title: Morphology of Flowering Plants
description: Grade 11 Biology: root, stem and leaf and their modifications, inflorescence, the flower, fruit and seed, floral formula/diagram, and the families Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae.

topics.title: The Root and the Stem
topics.concept:
Morphology is the study of the external form and structure of a plant. A typical flowering plant has an underground root system and an aerial shoot system (stem, leaves, flowers, fruits).

The Root. Roots are usually non-green, positively geotropic and grow underground. There are two main types: the tap root system (one main root with branches; in dicots, e.g. mustard) and the fibrous root system (a cluster of thin roots from the stem base; in monocots, e.g. wheat). Some plants have adventitious roots arising from parts other than the radicle (e.g. prop roots of banyan). A young root has four regions from tip upward: the root cap, the region of meristematic activity, the region of elongation, and the region of maturation (bearing root hairs). Roots are modified for special functions: storage (carrot, sweet potato — tuberous), support (prop roots of banyan, stilt roots of maize), and respiration (pneumatophores in mangroves like Rhizophora).

The Stem. The stem develops from the plumule, bears nodes (where leaves arise) and internodes, and is usually positively phototropic. It supports leaves, flowers and fruits, conducts water and food, and may store food or photosynthesise. Stems too are modified: underground stems for storage (potato tuber, ginger rhizome, onion bulb); sub-aerial stems for vegetative propagation (runner of grass, stolon, offset, sucker); and aerial modifications such as stem tendrils (for climbing, e.g. grapevine) and stem thorns (for defence, e.g. Citrus, Bougainvillea).

examples.problem: Example 1: Distinguish the tap root and fibrous root systems, with an example of each.
examples.solution:
Root systems differ between dicots and monocots.

  • Tap root: one main root with smaller branches; in dicots (e.g. mustard).
  • Fibrous root: a cluster of thin roots from the stem base; in monocots (e.g. wheat).
examples.answer: Tap root = a main root with branches (dicots, e.g. mustard); fibrous root = a cluster of thin roots from the stem base (monocots, e.g. wheat).

examples.problem: Example 2: What are pneumatophores and where are they found?
examples.solution:
Pneumatophores are a root modification for respiration.

  • They are roots that grow upward, out of the waterlogged soil.
  • They are found in mangrove plants (e.g. Rhizophora) and help in gas exchange (breathing).
examples.answer: Pneumatophores are upward-growing breathing roots of mangroves (e.g. Rhizophora) that help gas exchange in waterlogged soil.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give one example each of a stem modified for (a) storage and (b) climbing.
examples.solution:
Stems can be modified in many ways.

  • (a) Storage: potato tuber (or ginger rhizome).
  • (b) Climbing: stem tendril of grapevine.
examples.answer: (a) Storage: potato (tuber); (b) climbing: stem tendril of grapevine.

recap:
• Root systems: tap root (dicots) and fibrous root (monocots); adventitious roots arise from non-radicle parts.
  • Root regions: root cap, meristematic, elongation, maturation (root hairs).
  • Root modifications: storage (carrot), support (prop/stilt roots), respiration (pneumatophores).
  • Stem has nodes and internodes; modifications: underground (potato, ginger), sub-aerial (runner), tendrils, thorns.

quiz.q: The fibrous root system is characteristic of:
quiz.explanation: Monocots (e.g. wheat) typically have a fibrous root system.

quiz.q: A potato is an example of a modified:
quiz.explanation: The potato is an underground stem (tuber) modified for storage.

topics.title: The Leaf and the Inflorescence
topics.concept:
The Leaf is a flattened, green, lateral outgrowth of the stem that arises at a node. Its main function is photosynthesis. A typical leaf has three parts: the leaf base, the petiole (stalk) and the lamina (blade). Leaves may be simple (one undivided lamina) or compound (the lamina is divided into leaflets — pinnately compound like neem, or palmately compound like silk cotton).

Two features describe leaf arrangement and pattern:

  • Venation — the pattern of veins: reticulate (net-like, in dicots) or parallel (in monocots).
  • Phyllotaxy — the arrangement of leaves on the stem: alternate (one leaf per node, e.g. China rose), opposite (two per node) or whorled (more than two per node).

Leaves are also modified for special jobs: tendrils for climbing (pea), spines to reduce water loss/defence (cactus), storage (onion fleshy leaves), and even traps in insectivorous plants (pitcher plant).

The Inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis. There are two main types: racemose (the main axis keeps growing and flowers are borne laterally in an acropetal manner — older flowers at the bottom, e.g. mustard) and cymose (the main axis ends in a flower, so growth is limited; flowers open in a basipetal order — older flower in the centre/top).

examples.problem: Example 1: Differentiate reticulate and parallel venation, naming the plant group of each.
examples.solution:
Venation differs between dicots and monocots.

  • Reticulate: veins form a net-like pattern; in dicots.
  • Parallel: veins run parallel to each other; in monocots.
examples.answer: Reticulate (net-like) venation occurs in dicots; parallel venation occurs in monocots.

examples.problem: Example 2: Define phyllotaxy and name its three types.
examples.solution:
Phyllotaxy is the leaf arrangement.

  • It is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem.
  • Types: alternate, opposite and whorled.
examples.answer: Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on the stem; the three types are alternate, opposite and whorled.

examples.problem: Example 3: How does a racemose inflorescence differ from a cymose one?
examples.solution:
The difference is whether the main axis keeps growing.

  • Racemose: the main axis continues to grow; flowers open acropetally (older at the base), e.g. mustard.
  • Cymose: the main axis ends in a flower; flowers open basipetally (older in the centre).
examples.answer: In racemose the main axis keeps growing with flowers opening acropetally; in cymose the axis ends in a flower and flowers open basipetally.

recap:
• A leaf = leaf base + petiole + lamina; simple or compound (pinnate/palmate).
  • Venation: reticulate (dicots) vs parallel (monocots); phyllotaxy: alternate/opposite/whorled.
  • Leaf modifications: tendrils, spines, storage, insect traps.
  • Inflorescence: racemose (axis grows, acropetal) vs cymose (axis ends in a flower, basipetal).

quiz.q: Net-like (reticulate) venation is usually found in:
quiz.explanation: Dicots have reticulate venation; monocots have parallel venation.

quiz.q: In a racemose inflorescence, the flowers open in which order?
quiz.explanation: Racemose inflorescences open acropetally, with older flowers at the base.

topics.title: The Flower, Fruit, Seed and Plant Families
topics.concept:
The Flower is the reproductive unit of angiosperms, made of four whorls on the thalamus: calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens — male) and gynoecium (carpels/pistil — female). Useful terms: aestivation (the arrangement of sepals/petals in the bud — valvate, twisted, imbricate, vexillary) and placentation (the arrangement of ovules within the ovary — marginal, axile, parietal, basal, free-central).

After fertilisation, the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovule becomes the seed. A true fruit has a wall (pericarp) and seeds. A seed consists of a seed coat, an embryo (with radicle and plumule) and cotyledons; dicot seeds have two cotyledons, monocot seeds one (with endosperm).

A flower is summarised by a floral formula (using symbols for the whorls, their number and fusion) and a floral diagram (a cross-sectional sketch). Three important families:

  • Fabaceae (pea family) — flowers bisexual, zygomorphic; corolla papilionaceous (vexillary aestivation); 10 stamens (diadelphous); fruit a legume. Examples: pea, gram, groundnut. Economically very important (pulses, oil, nitrogen fixation).
  • Solanaceae (potato family) — flowers bisexual, actinomorphic; 5 fused sepals and petals; 5 stamens; bicarpellary, axile placentation; fruit a berry/capsule. Examples: potato, tomato, brinjal, tobacco.
  • Liliaceae (lily family) — typically monocots; flowers trimerous, actinomorphic; perianth of 6 tepals; 6 stamens; tricarpellary, axile placentation. Examples: onion, garlic, tulip, Aloe.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the four whorls of a typical flower and state which are reproductive.
examples.solution:
A flower has four whorls.

  • Calyx (sepals) and corolla (petals) — non-reproductive (accessory).
  • Androecium (stamens) and gynoecium (carpels) — reproductive.
examples.answer: Calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium; the reproductive whorls are the androecium and gynoecium.

examples.solution:
Both describe arrangements in the flower.

  • Aestivation: the arrangement of sepals or petals in the floral bud.
  • Placentation: the arrangement of ovules within the ovary.
examples.answer: Aestivation is the arrangement of sepals/petals in the bud; placentation is the arrangement of ovules within the ovary.

examples.problem: Example 3: To which family does the tomato belong, and name one feature of that family.
examples.solution:
Tomato is in the potato family.

  • Family: Solanaceae.
  • Feature: bisexual, actinomorphic flowers with axile placentation (fruit a berry).
examples.answer: Solanaceae; its flowers are bisexual and actinomorphic with axile placentation (fruit a berry).

recap:
• Flower whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium; aestivation (sepal/petal arrangement in bud) and placentation (ovule arrangement).
  • After fertilisation: ovary → fruit, ovule → seed.
  • A flower is summarised by a floral formula and floral diagram.
  • Families: Fabaceae (pea, legume), Solanaceae (potato/tomato), Liliaceae (onion, lily).

quiz.q: After fertilisation, the ovary of a flower develops into the:
quiz.explanation: The ovary becomes the fruit; the ovule becomes the seed.

quiz.q: The arrangement of ovules within the ovary is called:
quiz.explanation: Placentation is the arrangement of ovules inside the ovary.

questions.q: The study of the external form and structure of plants is:
questions.explanation: Morphology studies the external form and structure.

questions.q: The tap root system is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Dicots (e.g. mustard) have a tap root system.

questions.q: Roots that grow upward for gas exchange in mangroves are:
questions.explanation: Pneumatophores are breathing roots of mangroves.

questions.q: A potato is a modified:
questions.explanation: Potato is an underground stem tuber for storage.

questions.q: Stem tendrils, as in grapevine, help the plant to:
questions.explanation: Stem tendrils help in climbing.

questions.q: The three parts of a typical leaf are leaf base, lamina and:
questions.explanation: A leaf has a leaf base, petiole (stalk) and lamina (blade).

questions.q: Parallel venation is usually seen in:
questions.explanation: Monocots have parallel venation.

questions.q: The arrangement of leaves on a stem is called:
questions.explanation: Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on the stem.

questions.q: In a racemose inflorescence, the older flowers are at the:
questions.explanation: Racemose inflorescences open acropetally, older flowers at the base.

questions.q: The male reproductive whorl of a flower is the:
questions.explanation: The androecium (stamens) is the male whorl.

questions.q: The arrangement of sepals or petals in the floral bud is called:
questions.explanation: Aestivation is the arrangement of sepals/petals in the bud.

questions.q: The arrangement of ovules within the ovary is:
questions.explanation: Placentation is the arrangement of ovules in the ovary.

questions.q: Pea and gram belong to which family?
questions.explanation: Pea and gram are in the Fabaceae (pea family); fruit is a legume.

questions.q: Tomato and brinjal belong to the family:
questions.explanation: Tomato and brinjal are Solanaceae (potato family).

questions.q: Onion and garlic are members of the family:
questions.explanation: Onion and garlic are Liliaceae (lily family).

questions.q: A plant has a fibrous root system, parallel venation and trimerous flowers. It is most likely a:
questions.explanation: Fibrous roots, parallel venation and trimerous flowers are typical monocot features.

questions.q: Carrot and sweet potato both store food, but the carrot is a modified root while the sweet potato is a modified root too — what general purpose do such modifications serve?
questions.explanation: Tuberous/swollen roots are modified for storage of food and water.

questions.q: Why is the order of flower opening (acropetal vs basipetal) useful in classifying inflorescences?
options: It reflects whether the main axis keeps growing or ends in a flower
questions.explanation: Acropetal opening = racemose (axis grows on); basipetal = cymose (axis ends in a flower).

questions.q: A floral formula and a floral diagram together are useful because they:
options: Summarise the number, fusion and arrangement of floral parts compactly
Replace the need for the flower
questions.explanation: They compactly record the symmetry, whorls, numbers, fusion and position of floral parts.

questions.q: The Fabaceae are agriculturally vital partly because their roots host bacteria that:
options: Fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil
questions.explanation: Legume root nodules house nitrogen-fixing bacteria that enrich the soil.

questions.q: Two flowers both have fused petals and axile placentation, but one is regular (actinomorphic) and the other is irregular (zygomorphic). The zygomorphic one is more likely a:
questions.explanation: Fabaceae flowers are zygomorphic (papilionaceous), unlike the actinomorphic Solanaceae/Liliaceae.
